title: Don Quixote
body: Cervantes published his novel in two parts, in 1605 and 1615. The story of a man who has read too many tales of chivalry and sets out as a knight is often called the first modern novel.

title: The Divine Comedy
body: Dante Alighieri wrote the poem in the early 14th century. It follows a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. Written in Tuscan rather than Latin, it did much to shape the Italian literary language.

title: Impressionism
body: The movement took its name from Claude Monet's painting Impression, Sunrise, shown at an exhibition in Paris in 1874; a critic used the word mockingly. The Impressionists painted light and passing moments with visible brushstrokes, often outdoors.

title: War and Peace
body: Leo Tolstoy's novel, published in full in 1869, follows Russian aristocratic families through Napoleon's invasion of Russia. It mixes fiction with long reflections on history and is often counted among the greatest novels ever written.

title: The Sistine Chapel Ceiling
body: Michelangelo painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican between 1508 and 1512, including The Creation of Adam. The Last Judgment on the altar wall came later. The work is a high point of the High Renaissance.

title: Hamlet
body: Written around 1600, Hamlet is Shakespeare's longest play. The drama of the Danish prince who hesitates to avenge his father is among the most performed and analysed works in world literature.

title: The Iliad and the Odyssey
body: The two epic poems attributed to Homer date from around the 8th century BC. The Iliad tells of the Trojan War, the Odyssey of Odysseus' long journey home. They are the foundation of Western literature.

title: The Mona Lisa
body: Leonardo da Vinci worked on the portrait from about 1503 and kept it with him for years. Its soft transitions of light and shadow, known as sfumato, are much admired. It hangs in the Louvre and became world-famous partly after being stolen in 1911.

title: Guernica
body: Pablo Picasso painted Guernica in 1937 in response to the bombing of the Basque town during the Spanish Civil War. The huge black, white and grey canvas has become one of the best-known images against war. It hangs in the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

title: Pride and Prejudice
body: Jane Austen's novel of 1813 follows Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy. Its ironic portrait of marriage, money and class in English gentry society made it one of the most widely read novels in English.

title: Gothic Architecture
body: Gothic architecture emerged in France in the 12th century. Pointed arches, ribbed vaults and flying buttresses allowed taller buildings with large stained-glass windows, as in the cathedrals of Chartres and Notre-Dame de Paris.

title: The Night Watch
body: Rembrandt painted this group portrait of an Amsterdam militia company in 1642. Instead of a static row of figures he showed them in motion, with dramatic light. It is among the most famous works of the Dutch Golden Age and hangs in the Rijksmuseum.

title: Franz Kafka
body: In The Metamorphosis (1915) a man wakes up transformed into a giant insect. Kafka's stories of powerless individuals facing absurd systems gave rise to the word Kafkaesque. Much of his work was published after his death by his friend Max Brod, against his wishes.

title: A Doll's House
body: Henrik Ibsen's play of 1879 ends with Nora leaving her husband and children to find herself. The ending caused a scandal, and the play is a landmark of modern realist drama and of debates about women's place in marriage.

title: Cubism
body: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque developed Cubism around 1907–1914. Instead of a single viewpoint, they broke objects into geometric shapes seen from several angles at once. It was one of the most influential movements in modern art.
